html:
The map's label, in 1938 and 1945, for Portugal's colony of Mozambique on the south-east coast of Africa. Its longer history is told under Portuguese East Africa.

By the 1930s Portugal was ruled by the dictator Salazar, whose Estado Novo regime treated the colonies as part of the nation and as a source of raw materials. Large parts of Mozambique had been leased to chartered companies, which ruled them until the 1940s. From 1938 peasants in the north were forced to grow cotton for Portuguese mills, often at the cost of their own food. In the south, hundreds of thousands of men went to work in the mines of South Africa's Witwatersrand, and Portugal was paid in gold for their labour.

The capital, Lourenco Marques (now Maputo), grew as the port for the Transvaal. The liberation movement Frelimo began its war in 1964, and Mozambique became independent in 1975 after the Carnation Revolution in Lisbon.
